source: Galton (1907) Vox Populi, Nature 75:450-451 (read only through Wallis 2014, not the original)
finding: Founding study. At a Plymouth livestock fair, visitors paid 6d to guess the dressed weight of one ox. Galton took the median ('one vote one value'), not the mean, and found it close to the truth.
numbers: 787 usable cards (13 discarded). Published median 1207 lb, ox 1198 lb, error 9 lb (0.8%). Percentiles taken at 5,10,...,95.
quote: the vox populi was in this case 9 lb., or 0.8 per cent. of the whole weight too high
limits: The original scan has no text layer and I could not open it. Published figures were later shown to be slightly wrong (see a02). Paying entrants incl. butchers and farmers, so not a lay crowd.
agent_relevance: Origin story for 'a vote beats an individual'. It is one ox and one crowd with mixed expertise, so it is an anecdote, not a test of independence.

source: Wallis (2014) Revisiting Francis Galton's Forecasting Competition, Statistical Science 29(3)
finding: Went back to Galton's archive. The published numbers contain slips. Correct median is 1208 lb (394th of 787), correct dressed weight 1197 lb, so the median error was 11 lb (about 1%), not 9 lb.
numbers: Median 1208 (published 1207); outcome 1197 (published 1198); error 11 lb. Quartiles 1162 and 1236 (197th, 591st obs). Galton's probable error 37 lb = SD 54.9 lb.
limits: Draft says 1208; a typo fix changed the wrong digit. Galton never noticed; the errors went into his 1908 memoir.
agent_relevance: Even the founding number is repeated wrongly in most citations. Check numbers against the source before storing them as facts.

source: Wallis (2014), mean section
finding: The arithmetic mean of the 787 guesses was exactly the true weight. A correspondent (Hooker) had guessed the mean at about 1196 from Galton's percentile table; Galton replied the mean was 1197. Trimming the mean toward the median made the error larger.
numbers: Mean 1197 lb = outcome 1197 lb (error 0). Median error 11 lb. Hooker estimate 1196.
limits: One data set. The distribution was skewed, with tails fatter than a normal curve. Mean beat median here; in Lorenz 2011 (a08) the mean was bad and the geometric mean good.
agent_relevance: Choice of aggregator depends on the error distribution. For an agent that votes on numbers, check skew before averaging.

source: Wikipedia, Wisdom of the crowd (read through a summarising fetch tool)
finding: Summary of boundary conditions. Social influence can make a crowd average inaccurate; geometric mean and median are more robust. Averaging removes random but not systematic error. Groups seeking consensus can lose accuracy. Strategic voting and contrarian marginalisation hurt. Digital crowds are skewed by bots and heavy users.
numbers: Surprisingly popular method cut error 21.3% vs simple majority, 24.2% vs confidence-weighted, 22.2% vs advanced weighted. Rauhut and Lorenz: asking oneself infinitely often does not beat asking one other person.
limits: Tertiary source. Page returned Galton as 800 guessers and said the article lists no mean, which disagrees with Wallis (a02). Treat its numbers as pointers only.
agent_relevance: Gives the checklist of when a vote is not valid: shared bias, influence, strategic voting.

source: Condorcet (1785) Essay on the Application of Analysis to the Probability of Majority Decisions (read via Wikipedia, Condorcet's jury theorem)
finding: Formal core. A group decides by majority between two options. Each voter is right with independent probability p. If p > 1/2, adding voters raises the chance the majority is right and the limit is 1. If p < 1/2, more voters make it worse and one voter is best.
numbers: Example n=3, p=0.8: majority right with probability 0.896. Near p=1/2, P(n,p) grows linearly in p-1/2.
quote: each voter has an independent probability p of voting for the correct decision
limits: Assumes binary choice, independence, equal competence p. Later jury theorems relax these. Correlation breaks the limit-to-1 result (Ladha 1992, not opened).
agent_relevance: This is the exact claim behind G4: voting scales only if samples are independent and each better than chance. For a model sampled from one source, independence fails.

source: Page (2007) diversity prediction theorem, as stated in Lorenz et al. (2011)
finding: Identity: collective squared error = average individual squared error minus diversity (variance of guesses around the group mean). So a crowd beats its average member by exactly its diversity. It is arithmetic, not a social effect.
numbers: Formula as defined in Lorenz: collective error = squared deviation of group average from truth; diversity = average squared deviation from group average.
limits: Wikipedia has no page of this name (checked). Page's book not opened; only the definition via Lorenz. The identity holds for squared error and the mean only.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable quantity. If 5 samples all agree, diversity is 0, so the vote adds nothing beyond one sample.

source: Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer, Helbing (2011) How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect, PNAS 108(22)
finding: Lab test of the independence condition. 144 ETH students in 12 groups of 12 answered 6 factual estimation questions 5 times each, with money for accuracy. Conditions: no information, average of others, or full information. Social information shrank diversity but did not improve collective accuracy.
numbers: N=144, 12 sessions, 6 questions, 5 rounds. Payoff 4/2/1 points inside 10/20/40% of truth. Wisdom indicator about one unit lower with social information; aggregated information hurt more than full information. Confidence rose with no gain in accuracy.
limits: Students, trivia questions, groups of 12, mild influence. Real-world effect size unknown. Authors say the effect needs only mild influence.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G9 (no debate between samples): showing one sample another sample's answer cuts diversity without cutting error, and raises confidence.

source: Lorenz et al. (2011), aggregation results
finding: The arithmetic mean was bad because answers were right-skewed. Arithmetic mean was closer to truth than a random individual's first guess in only 21.3% of cases; the log-scale mean in 77.1%. Median and geometric mean were good.
numbers: Murders in Switzerland (true 198): arithmetic mean 838 (+323.2%), geometric 174 (-11.9%), median 170 (-14.1%). Population density (true 184): arithmetic 2,644 (+1,337%), geometric 132, median 130. Immigrants to Zurich (true 10,067): median 10,000 (-0.7%).
limits: Skew came from order-of-magnitude mistakes. Different question types may differ.
agent_relevance: When a model gives numeric answers, aggregate on a log scale or by median. A mean of samples can be worse than one sample.

source: Lorenz et al. (2011), range reduction and confidence effects
finding: Social influence moved the true value from the centre to the edge of the set of estimates ('range reduction'). Subjects also grew more confident without being more accurate ('confidence effect').
numbers: Wisdom indicator: truth inside the central 2, 4, 6... of 12 estimates; max 6; 0 means truth outside all estimates. Down by about 1 unit under influence.
limits: Confidence rated on a 6-point scale, only after round 1 and round 5.
agent_relevance: Agreement among samples can mean convergence, not truth. Never use the tightness of a cluster as a certainty signal alone (G4).

source: Hong and Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers, PNAS 101(46)
finding: Computational model. Agents search a ring of random values with different heuristics. A team of randomly chosen agents beats a team of the individually best agents, because the best agents become similar when the pool is large. 'Diversity trumps ability.'
numbers: Ring n=2000, k=3, l=12. Ten best vs ten random agents, 50 trials: performance 92.56 vs 94.53; diversity 70.98% vs 90.99%. Twenty agents: 93.78 vs 94.72. l=20: 93.52 vs 96.08 (diversity 73.69% vs 94.31%). Single run: best agents 93.2, random 94.7.
limits: Needs the pool of heuristics to be finite and agents identical in perspective. Later critiques (Thompson 2014, Grim et al. 2018; both listed, not opened) say the theorem needs strong assumptions. Random beats best only when ability gap is small (scores 84-87).
agent_relevance: Supports selecting different strategies over copies of the best one, but only where the answer is found by search. For single-answer vote tasks G4 says persona voters do not help.

source: Hong and Page (2004), theorem framing
finding: A group can only get stuck on a solution that is a local optimum of every member. So different heuristics shrink the shared stuck set. This holds whatever the teamwork rule.
numbers: Hiring example: 1,000 applicants with scores 60-90%; compare best 1, next-best 20, or random 20.
limits: Agents of 'limited ability' with scores in a narrow band. Result is about search, not about voting on a fact.
agent_relevance: For search over candidates, independent heuristics widen coverage; for one-answer questions this is not the same as a vote.

source: Surprisingly Popular algorithm, Prelec, Seung and McCoy (2017) Nature 541 (numbers read through Wikipedia only)
finding: Choose the answer that is more popular than people predicted it would be. Works when a minority knows the truth and also knows the majority will be wrong.
numbers: Error cut 21.3% vs majority, 24.2% vs confidence-weighted, 22.2% vs advanced (as reported on Wikipedia, not checked in paper).
limits: Paper behind a paywall; I could not open it. Needs an expert minority. See a18 for LLM test.
agent_relevance: A candidate way to pick an answer without ground truth, but only if some samples know better than the majority.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd, arXiv 2402.19379 (Science Advances 2024)
finding: Preregistered test. Median of 12 LLMs on 31 binary forecasting questions was statistically no different from 925 human forecasters, and beat a 50% no-information baseline.
numbers: 12 LLMs, 31 questions, 925 humans, 3-month tournament. Acquiescence: mean model forecast reliably above 50% though outcomes were nearly evenly split. Study 2: giving GPT-4 or Claude 2 the median human forecast raised accuracy by 17-28%; averaging human and machine was better still.
limits: Only 31 questions. Models from different families, not copies of one. Training cutoff contamination was not ruled out here (see a20).
agent_relevance: Shows diverse-family aggregation can match a human crowd. The shared bias (acquiescence) is a systematic error that no averaging fixes.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning, ICLR (arXiv 2203.11171)
finding: Sample many reasoning paths from one model and take the most frequent final answer. Large gains on arithmetic and commonsense tasks where answers are checkable and have one final value.
numbers: Gains over greedy chain of thought: GSM8K +17.9%, SVAMP +11.0%, AQuA +12.2%, StrategyQA +6.4%, ARC-challenge +3.9%.
limits: Paths come from one model so errors are correlated; the gain is real but smaller than independent-voter theory predicts. Needs a final answer that can be matched exactly.
agent_relevance: The practical base for our vote step. It works because the right answer is more common than any single wrong answer, not because samples are independent.

source: Li et al. (2024) More agents is all you need (Agent Forest), TMLR, arXiv 2402.05120
finding: Sampling and voting scales with the number of agents. Smaller models with enough votes can match bigger ones. Gain is larger on harder tasks and weaker models.
numbers: Ensemble size 40: GSM8K +12 to +24 points, MATH +6 to +10, Chess +1 to +4, MMLU +5 to +11, HumanEval +4 to +9. Llama2-13B at 15 agents about equals Llama2-70B single on GSM8K.
limits: Gains are on checkable benchmarks; shrinks near ceiling. No test of independence. Paper describes difficulty effects, not correlation.
agent_relevance: Shows the vote works on average for benchmark tasks. Check against a16-a24 for the conditions that remove the gain.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated errors in large language models, ICML 267, arXiv 2506.07962
finding: Large-scale measure of independence. Models agree on wrong answers far more than chance. Same provider, same architecture and similar size raise error correlation. More accurate models have more correlated errors, even across providers.
numbers: 349 LLMs on 12,032 multiple-choice questions (HuggingFace leaderboard); 71 LLMs on 14,042 (HELM); 20 LLMs on 1,800 resume-job pairs. HELM: models agree about 60% of the time when both are wrong; random choice among 3 wrong answers gives 33%. HuggingFace random baseline 0.127. Features explain 34-62% of variation in error agreement.
limits: Multiple-choice and resume tasks. Open-ended answers may differ. Agreement among wrong answers counts only when both err.
agent_relevance: Core evidence that different LLMs are not independent voters, and newer stronger models are more alike. Supports G4.

source: Kim et al. (2025), downstream effects
finding: When one LLM judges another, the judge over-credits models that are less accurate than it, especially same-provider or same-architecture ones. In hiring, correlated models make the same wrong decisions (monoculture).
numbers: 20 LLMs on 1,800 resume pairs; residual correlation measured against human labels.
limits: Judge numbers not extracted in detail here.
agent_relevance: A model grading its own kind misses shared mistakes. Use a different kind of check for selection, not a copy.

source: Denisov-Blanch, Kazdan et al. (2026) Consensus is not verification, arXiv 2603.06612
finding: Polling-style aggregation does not improve truthfulness on unverifiable tasks. Across five benchmarks and several models, even at 25 times the inference cost, majority vote, confidence weighting and Surprisingly Popular give no consistent gain and often amplify shared misconceptions. Forecasting questions after the model cutoff are at chance.
numbers: Five benchmarks; 25x sampling cost. MATH plurality-wrong rate 3.9-25.8%, and the most common wrong answer is 65-87% of wrong responses. AIME plurality-wrong 3.9-75.8%, error concentration 20-63%. Temperature 0.7 to 1.0 flips the plurality answer in only 2.9% of question-model pairs. Inverse-SP gets 80% on HLE but is at chance elsewhere.
limits: Preprint. Gains in math survive because a verifier filters answers, which the authors say agrees with prior work. Some figures read from extracted text with lost dashes.
agent_relevance: Best statement of when a vote is not valid: no verifier plus correlated errors. Samples at higher temperature are still not independent hypotheses.

source: Denisov-Blanch et al. (2026), diagnostics
finding: Models agree with each other more than with truth. Correlation between model answers is positive on every dataset but correlation with truth varies by task. Self-reported confidence tracks agreement, not correctness. The Surprisingly Popular signal flips sign between benchmarks.
numbers: Pearson correlation figures on HLE, Predict-the-Future and BoolQ (values in figures, not read). Even out-of-distribution random strings give correlated outputs across models.
limits: Figure values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Do not use verbal confidence or sample agreement as a stop rule alone (matches SCHEMA guardrail G4).

source: Douven (2026) Wisdom of LLM crowds: aggregation and contamination, ACM Trans. Soc. Comput., arXiv 2607.18269
finding: 15 LLMs gave probabilities on 254 binary prediction-market questions. A logistic regression over model outputs, trained on earlier items, beat every single model and the mean. Its useful signal was model disagreement. Training-cutoff contamination was a big confound.
numbers: Clean subset 94 items. Brier: logistic 0.241, MLP 0.264, arithmetic mean 0.313; accuracy 0.511 for the mean vs 0.606 MLP. Gap between cloud and local models fell from 35.8% to 8.9% on clean items. Best single model Brier about 0.284 (Claude Opus 4.6) and 0.286 (Gemini Flash).
limits: Crowd of 15 models, one question type. Learned aggregator needs resolved historic items. Even market-at-cutoff comparison left LLMs less accurate.
agent_relevance: A simple weighted combination, not a plain average, beat the best model. Rankings of models were only moderately stable, so avoid choosing one voter by past score.

source: Chetlapalli, Liao, Chen, Chen (2026) Diverse by reasoning: wisdom of LLM crowds for future prediction, arXiv 2608.24001
finding: Cluster 25 LLMs by how they reason, pick one medoid per cluster. A 3-model crowd beat voting over all 25 on both forecasting benchmarks. Crowd composition mattered more than size; maximising diversity was not best, representative coverage was.
numbers: 25 LLMs, 350 questions from 7 development benchmarks for clustering, 2 future-prediction benchmarks for test. 88% fewer model calls, about 80% lower inference cost than 25-model voting.
limits: Preprint; exact accuracy deltas not extracted. Clustering uses reasoning traces from other tasks.
agent_relevance: Supports selecting voters for different behaviour, not adding more of the same.

source: Ai, Pan, Simchi-Levi, Tambe, Xu (2026) Beyond majority voting: LLM aggregation by leveraging higher-order information, arXiv 2510.01499
finding: Two label-free weights (Optimal Weight, Inverse Surprising Popularity) use each model's expected accuracy and the correlation between answers. They provably fix limits of majority vote under mild assumptions and beat it empirically.
numbers: Correctly answers questions that majority vote misses: 5.22% UltraFeedback, 9.83% MMLU, 3.66% ARMMAN. t-statistics vs MV: 12.53, 23.39, 3.22 (all p<0.001). Beats all single models on UltraFeedback and ARMMAN.
limits: Needs several different models, uses the pool's own statistics. Authors note the single best model is an oracle baseline.
agent_relevance: If we ever vote across different models, weighting by pairwise correlation is a stronger option than plain majority.

source: Barrera-Lemarchand, Sigman, Navajas (2026) The wisdom of artificial deliberative crowds, arXiv 2609.22497
finding: Three-stage deliberation (answer alone, discuss in groups of three, answer again) from human work. Across four tasks, consensus of heterogeneous model groups had lower error than averaging their independent answers. Groups of three copies of one model did not benefit.
numbers: Study 1 (disks in a jar, 14 pictures): consensus squared error 0.164 vs 0.195 for the group mean (paired d=0.40, p=9.8e-8); individual error 0.230 to 0.159 after deliberation (d=0.40). 12 consensus values vs 36 individual values: d=4.75. Homogeneous Anthropic groups: z=1.22, p=0.22, no gain. Studies 2-4: NeurIPS review (100 papers), agent safety (50 trajectories), World Cup 2026 forecasts.
limits: Estimation tasks with numeric answers; heterogeneous models from three families. Conflicts in direction with Lorenz 2011 (a07) where influence hurt humans; here groups were small, structured and diverse.
agent_relevance: Deliberation helps only when members differ. This does not contradict G9 for clones of one model, which is the case here.

source: Hidden clones, arXiv 2603.17111 (2026) Family bias in vision-language model ensembles
finding: 17 VLMs from 8 families behave like fewer than 3 independent voters. Same-family errors correlate more than cross-family. A 'Misleading' tier of questions exists where correlated majority wrong answers collapse calibrated voting to 0% though the best model is right.
numbers: VQAv2 N=20,001, TextVQA 5,000, GQA 12,578. Within-family r=0.67 +/-0.12, cross-family r=0.53 +/-0.07 (p<0.001). Participation ratio 2.86 effective voters; first component 58.0% of variance. Misleading tier 2.5% of VQAv2: best model 78.9%, calibrated vote 0.0%, family-hierarchical voting 26.0%.
limits: Vision-language, not text. Preprint. Hierarchical voting method proposed by the authors themselves.
agent_relevance: A direct measure of how many independent voters a model pool is worth. Sampling 17 outputs does not give 17 votes.

source: Latent dimension of Condorcet's jury theorem for multiple AI advisers, arXiv 2609.14438 (2026)
finding: Even with ideal independent competent advisers, the chance that at least some advisers visibly disagree rises toward 1 as the panel grows. Reliability and visible dissent cross at adviser accuracy 0.8; below it, dissent becomes more likely than a correct majority.
numbers: Binomial model; crossing point at 4/5 accuracy.
limits: Theory only; assumes independence. Applies to how disagreement is shown to a user.
agent_relevance: A split vote does not by itself mean the vote failed. Do not treat dissent among samples as a sign of error.

source: Condorcet theorem with correlated votes (Ladha 1992; list from OpenAlex, not opened)
finding: Ladha (1992) 'The Condorcet jury theorem, free speech, and correlated votes' extends the theorem to correlated voters; the known result is that correlation can cap group accuracy below 1.
numbers: Titles and years only (OpenAlex): Ladha 1992, 475 citations.
limits: Not opened. The cap claim comes from my background knowledge, not from this session.
agent_relevance: Mathematical basis for why shared training error limits what a vote can achieve.

source: Social influence undermines wisdom in sequential decision making (Management Science 2020; list only)
finding: A later paper reports that social influence undermines crowd wisdom in sequential decision making. Title suggests the Lorenz effect extends beyond one-shot estimates.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only title and year seen. Needs opening before use.
agent_relevance: Open question: do the Lorenz effects hold for sequential answer chains, like an agent reading its own earlier answers?

source: Examining independence in ensemble sentiment analysis with LLMs via the Condorcet jury theorem (SSRN 5199096, 2025; list only)
finding: Paper title says it examines independence in ensemble sentiment analysis with LLMs using Condorcet's theorem.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only title seen.
agent_relevance: Another test of the same question; follow up in angle B.
